analysis.one_liner: Lets workers over 40 take age discrimination claims to court instead of forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate committee approved the bill in May 2024, but it never received a Senate floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Most older workers sign contracts that force any future age discrimination claim into private arbitration, where there is no jury, no public record, and no class action. This bill would void those pre-signed agreements for age discrimination claims, letting workers choose to sue in court. It cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee with bipartisan support and was placed on the Senate's calendar, but the Senate never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers age 40 and older who face age discrimination on the job. If the bill passed, they could elect to take their claim to a federal or state court, with a judge deciding whether the bill applies, rather than being funneled into a private arbitration process set up by their employer.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes pre-dispute arbitration agreements and pre-dispute class-action waivers unenforceable for age discrimination claims, but only at the worker's election — a worker who prefers arbitration can still use it.
It defines covered disputes broadly, including disparate treatment, disparate impact, harassment, and retaliation against anyone 40 or older under federal, tribal, state, or local law.

It gives the choice to the person alleging discrimination or the representative of a class, and requires a court — not an arbitrator — to decide whether the law applies, closing a common loophole where employers write contracts that hand that decision to the arbitrator themselves.
It applies only to claims arising after enactment, so existing signed agreements stay valid for disputes that already accrued.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would face more age discrimination lawsuits in open court — jury trials, public records, and possible class actions — instead of confidential arbitration they currently control. Private arbitration firms also lose this stream of disputes.

drawbacks.text: Employers and business groups have long argued that arbitration resolves employment disputes faster and more cheaply for both sides than court litigation, and that court cases can take years. That is a real trade-off, not an empty objection.

The bill is narrow: it covers only age discrimination claims. It does nothing about forced arbitration for race discrimination, disability discrimination, wage theft, or other workplace claims, so most forced arbitration agreements remain fully enforceable outside this one category.
Voiding pre-dispute class and joint-action waivers for age claims could encourage more class litigation, which raises costs for employers and is one reason business groups oppose arbitration limits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For older workers the benefit is substantial: their age discrimination claim stops being decided in a private forum with no jury, no public record, and no ability to band together, and the employer's own contract can no longer hand the key legal decisions to its chosen arbitrator. The cost — more courtroom litigation for employers — is real but is the point of the change: it is what makes the process public and adversarial. The bill's narrowness is its honest weakness; it fixes one slice of forced arbitration and leaves the rest untouched.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved it with bipartisan support and placed it on the Senate's calendar, but the Senate leadership never brought it to the floor for a vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced June 14, 2023 by Senator Gillibrand with 13 other original cosponsors from both parties, and was referred to the Judiciary Committee.
On May 9, 2024 the Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment, and on May 16, 2024 it was formally reported to the Senate.
The same day, it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders — a list of bills awaiting floor time — but no floor debate or vote ever followed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that use forced arbitration for age discrimination claims keep that shield: a claim their worker signs away before a dispute ever arises stays out of court, out of the public record, and out of class actions. Private arbitration firms keep the business as well.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers using forced arbitration keep the shield

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 14, 2023 and recruited a bipartisan list of original cosponsors.

for.name: Sen. Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill out of committee without amendment on May 16, 2024.

for.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment on May 9, 2024.

for.name: Bipartisan original cosponsors including Sens. Graham, Grassley, and Hawley
for.what_they_did: Signed onto the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought S. 1979 up for a floor vote despite its placement on the Senate calendar in May 2024; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and employer groups
against.what_they_did: Have long opposed bills restricting pre-dispute arbitration agreements in employment, arguing arbitration is faster and cheaper for resolving workplace disputes.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was genuinely bipartisan — of its 14 original cosponsors, 3 were Republicans including Sens. Graham, Grassley, and Hawley, alongside 10 Democrats, and the committee approved it without recorded opposition; the obstacle was floor time, not a party-line vote.

industries.note: Employers currently rely on pre-signed arbitration agreements to keep age discrimination claims out of court, where a jury and a public record await. The bill removes that shield for the 40-plus workforce, which is why employer groups oppose arbitration limits generally.
Arbitration firms would lose age discrimination disputes, a source of paid-for appointments, if those claims move to public courts instead.
Employment lawyers representing older workers would gain court cases — including possible class actions — that arbitration agreements currently block.
